notes.display: The first part of this question, on proof by contradiction, included a partially completed attempt at showing that if $n^3$ is even, then $n$ is even.

notes.quote: It was there to help candidates solve part (b), by not only giving them the structure of a proof, but also the key steps in helping them solve it.
A great many responses to part (a) did correctly factorise the expression, but few made a comment to state that it was odd. Both of these aspects were required to show the contradiction.
Responses to part (b) were mixed with many not understanding the meaning of a rational or irrational number.
For those who did make a start and stated the contradiction ''There exists integers a and b such that 3 2 a b = '' many went on to gain two or three marks out of 5.
notes.display: For those who did make a start and stated the contradiction "There exists integers $a$ and $b$ such that $\sqrt[3]{2}=\dfrac{a}{b}$" many went on to gain two or three marks out of 5.

notes.quote: Most of these forgot, however, to add a statement that a b was fully simplified which would mean that the last mark in the question could not be awarded.

It is really important in a proof to include all necessary steps, and in this one it was common to see '' 3 3 3 3 3 2 2 2 a a a b b b = ⇒ = ⇒ = '' followed by ''hence a is even'' rather than '' 3 3 3 3 3 2 2 2 a a a b b b = ⇒ = ⇒ = '' followed by ''hence a3 is even so a is even'' (using part a) The final part of the proof could then be reached by setting 2 a m = , before substituting this into 3 3 2 a b = to give ''( )3 3 3 3 2 2 4 m b b m = ⇒ = followed by the same deduction that b3 is even so b is even'' The order of the statements was crucial to scoring full marks, as was the fact that a and b had no common factors in the initial statement.
notes.display: It is really important in a proof to include all necessary steps, and in this one it was common to see "$\sqrt[3]{2}=\dfrac{a}{b}\Rightarrow 2=\dfrac{a^3}{b^3}\Rightarrow a^3=2b^3$" followed by "hence $a$ is even" rather than "$\sqrt[3]{2}=\dfrac{a}{b}\Rightarrow 2=\dfrac{a^3}{b^3}\Rightarrow a^3=2b^3$" followed by "hence $a^3$ is even so $a$ is even" (using part a) The final part of the proof could then be reached by setting $a=2m$, before substituting this into $a^3=2b^3$ to give "$(2m)^3=2b^3\Rightarrow b^3=4m^3$ followed by the same deduction that $b^3$ is even so $b$ is even" The order of the statements was crucial to scoring full marks, as was the fact that $a$ and $b$ had no common factors in the initial statement.

notes.quote: As a result fully correct proofs were rare and only awarded to the best of candidates.
